rv.q: I left this lovely, subtle, intelligent show in a melancholy daze.
It is a production of piercing lyricism as well as embracing warmth and wit: gorgeous.
A beautiful production of a beautiful play.
Rourke’s production is beautifully pitched: even as the women tease and bicker, and coax music out of their erratic new wireless, there’s a shadow of sadness to it.
Josie Rourke’s sumptuous and thoughtful staging of Dancing at Lughnasa shows why this 1990 play is so loved.

Movement lies at the emotional heart of this play and it is orchestrated with such delicate mastery by Wayne McGregor that the stomping scene, featuring the sisters dancing with wild abandon is a shared hedonistic escape, rebellious ritual and act of worship in one.
In a glorious performance of quiet luminosity, Mitchell gradually unpeels layers of the seemingly strait-laced Kate's complexity...
Mostly the play works brilliantly across many levels.

The performances – from Justice Mitchell’s hardbitten, scolding eldest Kate, to Ardal O’Hanlon’s endearingly confused Jack – can’t be faulted but, like that temperamental Marconi, their full force is felt a tad too intermittently.
Despite the epic scale and beauty of Robert Jones’s set, the opening moments feels surprisingly understated.
The evening is bathed in charm and quiet desolation but it seldom rises above the merely watchable.
Yet I still find the piece, even when it’s performed with conviction, as it is here, naggingly schematic and sometimes shamelessly sentimental.
I was left pining for the gut-churning conflict of loss and longing that can make Friel's writing a great deal more potent.
It is a glory, full of emotion and power.

Now, Josie Rourke repeats the feat with Friel’s 1990. Olivier and Tony-winning play Dancing at Lughnasa, featuring a spellbinding cast with some popular sitcom names: Siobhán McSweeney and Louisa Harland from Derry Girls, and Father Ted’s Ardal O’Hanlon.
This whole play becomes a sharing, feeling the frustrations and fears of the Mundy and their enthusiastic breakout to find release in dancing.
Dancing at Lughnasa definitely deserves the moniker.
Brian Friel’s 1990 play set during harvest time at the village of Ballybeg somewhere in County Donegal, is intensely evocative of a world which has almost entirely disappeared.
And yet the genius of this play is to enfold its sorrow in a profound, empathic embrace that acts most definitely as a homage to family members viewed throughout with fondness.
There are excellent performances from the five sisters in this engaging and deeply reflective show.
Ultimately one wonders what director, Josie Rourke, intended to make of the work in its second production at The National Theatre, having also played at The Old Vic in 2009 and around the world.
Famine zones are more fun than this play and yet Brian Friel's shrieking bumpkins are exactly what the Arts Council wants us to see.
This is the only play this year I’d willingly see again soon.

Utterly captivating and at times unconventional in its approach, its refreshingly different storytelling device, impressive set design and truly outstanding cast ensure this is an overall winning show which delicately balances the joy in life with the uncertainty and fragility of the future.
Friel's language never fails to move and this is a poignant evocation of familial love and times long past.

cn.t: Friel's memory play receives a sumptuous, detailed revival that mostly captivates critics with its evocative design and strong ensemble cast, though some find it overly sentimental or question its contemporary relevance.

vr.q: I give this production of Dancing at Lunis at the National Theater four stars.
